1:
The crime charged against Moab is a desecration, and they differ on how much of the story can be recovered. Henry supplies the background: there was war between Moab and Edom, and the Moabite king in distress offered his own son as a burnt-offering to appease his deity; afterwards he or a successor did what is charged here, the cruelty aimed not at the people of God but at a heathen like himself. Ellicott is more cautious. He corrects the rendering to burned to lime the bones of the king of Edom, calls the historical reference obscure, and says it cannot be determined whether Moab desecrated royal tombs or offered the heir of Edom in sacrifice. Wesley gives the most concrete version: the bones reduced by fire to fine dust and the ashes used instead of lime to plaster the walls and roofs of the palace, in hatred and contempt. Clarke suspects some brutality without specifying it; Gill supplies the ancestry of the nation and its record of enmity, sending for a diviner to curse Israel and oppressing them in the days of the judges. Calvin reports a reading he does not adopt, that some take the bones for courage, as though the king's whole strength had been consumed.

Calvin states the formula's logic, which governs the whole series of oracles. The prophet charges the Moabites with perverseness, wholly given over and past hope of repentance, having added crimes to crimes and reached the highest pitch of wickedness, which is what the numbering imports; from this we learn that vengeance did not come hastily, their wickedness having become intolerable before it fell. Clarke gives the chapter's plan: judgments against Moab, then Judah, then Israel as the particular object of the prophet's mission, their sins aggravated by God's distinguishing regard.

The city named in the sentence is identified by three of them. Clarke calls it a principal city of the Moabites and reads the following clauses as marking a capture by storm and a total slaughter. Wesley agrees and glosses the tumult as the noise soldiers make when they carry all by force. Ellicott notes that the name properly signifies a group of towns but is used here of a single large town, which he identifies with a modern site. Gill leaves open whether the fire falls on the country or on a city of the same name, and names the invader. Calvin declines the geography and draws the sense: God would consume them by violent punishment as by fire, fortified places could not hinder his vengeance, and though proud of their palaces these would avail them nothing; the tumult and shouting mean the enemy would take every fortified city by force.

The cutting off of the judge is the one substantial disagreement, and it is about scope. Gill takes the judge for the principal governor, the king, since kings have sometimes taken the bench and administered justice themselves. Clarke reads it as the abolition of government itself, so the place shall never more have any form of it, and notes that the Hebrew for judge may signify chief magistrate, the chief magistrates of Carthage bearing a title probably taken from it. Wesley reads the singular distributively, meaning every one of them. Calvin makes the sentence a national extinction rather than a constitutional one. Men cannot exist as a body without civil government, and wherever men are assembled there must be princes to rule them; so to say there shall be no more a judge among the Moabites is to say their name would be blotted out, since had the people continued some princes must have remained. When the princes are destroyed the people perish too, for they have no security; the threat is therefore not temporary. Keil and Delitzsch supply the transition, the oracle turning from Moab to Judah, whose charge is despising the law.
4:
The turn from the heathen to the covenant people is what all of them notice first. Gill says the prophet proceeds from the nations round about to the people of God, for whose ill usage those nations were chiefly threatened, lest Judah promise itself impunity; had they considered rightly they could not have expected it, since if heathen ignorant of the law were punished, much more those who knew it and did it not. Calvin makes the same argument from the saying that a servant who knows his master's will and does it not is worthy of many stripes: what was said of the uncircumcised was a prelude to the destruction near the chosen people, and God could not forgive the children of Abraham when he had spared none of the others. Ellicott states it as a bare principle: high privilege does not involve immunity, and Judah shall be chastised with the same penalty as Edom and Philistia and Ammon and Moab. Gill specifies that Judah here includes Benjamin, the two tribes distinguished from the ten who follow.

The charge against Judah is itemised by two of them. Clarke divides it under three heads, that they despised or rejected the law, that they kept not the statutes, and that they followed lies, being idolaters who preferred false prophets to those sent by God; he adds that the three and four may be taken to any latitude, the people having lived in continual hostility to their God from the days of David to the reign under which this prophet spoke. Wesley glosses the lies as idols, and explains the erring as caused partly by the natural tendency of the sin and partly by the just judgment of God; the walking after them he takes successively, one generation after another. On the sentence itself Gill and Clarke agree in naming the same invader, and Clarke specifies the war that ended in the sacking and burning of the city and its temple.

The address then narrows to Israel, and Calvin explains the design. The prophet omits all reference to other nations, since his business was with those he was appointed to teach; but he wished first to set God's judgment before them as in a series of mirrors, and to exhibit in the Jews themselves an example of extreme vengeance, though there was greater purity and a purer religion still among them. Keil and Delitzsch note the form, that the judgment on Israel is announced as irrevocable in precisely the same terms used of the nations already named, with a fuller description of the sins following. Gill identifies the ten tribes by their history, rent from the house of David and departing from the true worship to set up calves at two shrines.

The selling of the righteous produces the tile's real dispute, and Ellicott names his opponents. He holds it clear, by comparison with a later chapter, that the Jewish interpreters, followed by one modern scholar, were incorrect in charging the sin on corrupt judges who by bribery delivered unjust judgments against the righteous; the sin consists rather in the perverse straining of the law that allowed an insolvent debtor to sell himself into bondage to redeem a debt. Clarke takes exactly the reading Ellicott rejects, that the judges were mercenary and corrupt, taking bribes to condemn the righteous and even for articles of clothing such as a pair of shoes condemning the poor man and delivering him to his adversary; he adds a second head, that they were unmerciful to the poor generally, and observes that the whole history of this people is one tissue of transgression, so that one may open the historical or prophetic books at any point to be satisfied of their delinquency. Wesley says only that the shoes stand proverbially for the smallest bribe, which sides with the judicial reading without argument.
7:
Panting after the dust on the head of the poor is a crux and none of them hide it. Calvin says the place is not well understood, and works from the verb, which means to pant and is often used of desiring. Some render it that they desire the heads of the poor to be in the dust; he calls that strained. Gill leaves both open: either they were greedy after money, the dust of the earth, and could not endure that the poor should keep their little of it, or they were eager to drag them through the dust until they were suppliants with their mouths in it. Ellicott follows two named scholars: they long to see the poor so distressed that dust is thrown on their heads in token of grief, the meek defrauded as too weak to claim their own. Wesley reads it the same way, glossing the turning aside as maliciously interpreting the designs of the humble.

The clause about the maid is read as cultic, not merely lewd. Ellicott identifies the woman as the prostitute devoted to the ritual of a goddess, takes the clause to point at the sensuality of the popular worship, and holds the prophet regards the obscenity as a deliberate desecration of the divine name. Wesley reads it as the corrupt judges committing a lewdness the heathen abhor. Keil and Delitzsch mark the aggravation, that such contempt of the commandments was highly reprehensible in itself.

The pledged garments are explained from law and temple custom. Gill notes that clothes taken in pledge should have been restored before sunset, and that these were spread by the altars raised to idols and slept on as on carpets, as was usual among the Gentiles, who lay so in the temples of their gods to obtain good dreams. Wesley adds that they leaned rather than sat upright at meals, and identifies the drink-offerings as bought with fines laid on the innocent. Ellicott sets the verse beside the law, corrects the rendering to upon garments received in pledge they stretch themselves, and would adopt the marginal mulcted for condemned, the money wrung from those who could not pay being spent in rioting; the Greek reads it very differently, but the received text is justified by four other ancient versions. Calvin addresses the charge to the chief men, since the common people could not have feasted on spoils gained by judicial proceedings, and recalls that the law forbade taking from a poor man a pledge he needed for daily use.

The recital of mercies is treated by all as the aggravation of the charge. Gill lists the driving out of the seven nations, the Amorite standing here for the rest. Clarke enumerates five heads: the bringing out of Egypt, the sustaining forty years in the wilderness, the driving out of the Canaanites, the raising up of prophets, and the institution of the Nazarites. Henry draws the moral: we need often to be reminded of mercies received, which are the heaviest aggravations of sins committed; and though God gives liberally and does not upbraid us with our unworthiness, he justly upbraids us with ingratitude. Calvin says the same in his own key: God complains he had ill bestowed his blessings and was defrauded by those for whose sake he had done so much, who acted as if they were like other nations and not bound to him by adoption. Ellicott turns to the history, putting the emphasis on the pronoun, placing the Amorites proper on the south-western coast of the Dead Sea, and noting that their stature was sometimes attributed to all the land's inhabitants, and that they had been absorbed before this prophet's time. Wesley calls them the mightiest of the Canaanites, takes the oaks for a proverbial figure of strength, and reads the fruit and roots as the children and the old standards.
10:
The redemption from Egypt is recited as the second head of the indictment, and Calvin explains why it is dwelt on at such length. Men for the most part extenuate the favours of God, an evil innate in us, which is the reason the prophet describes and extols the redemption so largely; they ought to have remembered their condition in Egypt, where they were most miserably oppressed, so that setting the coming out before them was the same as reminding them of that. Gill says the same briefly, that they were bond slaves in great affliction and unable to help themselves, and were brought out of that house of bondage with a high hand. Keil and Delitzsch add the further point the verses make, that God had not only put Israel in possession of the land but had continually shown himself the founder and promoter of its spiritual prosperity. Ellicott alone turns to the forty years and gives them a double character: the wandering was a punishment for fickleness and cowardice, but during the incidence of that judgment, of which only one or two events are recorded, God was disciplining and organising a tribe of restless wanderers into a nation.

The prophets and Nazarites are the third head, and the expositors divide the labour. Gill names examples among the prophets and describes their office as not merely foretelling but teaching the doctrines and duties of religion and warning the people of their sins and the danger of them. Wesley defines the other order, persons who bound themselves to a very sober and holy life, either for a set time or for their whole life. Calvin makes the raising up of prophets a remarkable proof of divine love in itself, and draws out why: if God were to speak himself from heaven or send his angels down it would appear much more dignified, yet he condescends to guide his people by men; and he notes in passing that the Hebrew word behind young men means chosen men, and that the particle opening the clause may be either a simple affirmation or an addition.

The charge that follows turns those mercies into the measure of the offence. Gill has them either persuade or force the Nazarites to drink, contrary to their vow and calling and in contempt of it, in order to make them like themselves. Wesley says they importuned them to drink, to violate their vow and contemn God's law. Clarke notes that the thing was expressly forbidden in the laws of that institution, and adds the parallel refusal, that they would neither worship God nor hear the voice of his prophets.

Calvin anticipates an objection at exactly this point, and it is the most interesting passage in the tile. It seems a light offence that wine was given to the Nazarites, since the kingdom of God is not meat and drink; and though the apostle's saying to that effect had not yet been uttered, it was true in every age. Wine was in itself lawful, provided it was used with moderation. The answer he gives is simple: it was lawful to drink wine, but these had of their own accord undertaken to abstain from it, and the offence lies in the violation of what was voluntarily vowed rather than in the thing itself. Keil and Delitzsch state the consequence without the argument, that the Lord would visit this base contempt of covenant mercies with severe punishment, and paraphrase the sentence that follows as a pressing down like that of a cart filled with sheaves; they carry the paraphrase forward into the loss of flight to the swift, the strong man unable to fortify his strength, and the hero unable to deliver his own soul.
13:
The image of the loaded cart is the chapter's last real crux, and it turns on whether one verb is active or passive. Gill takes the passive sense without hesitation: God is pressed under them with the weight of their sins, with which they had made him to serve and had wearied him, his patience quite worn out so that he could bear them no longer. Calvin sets out both possibilities honestly. The Hebrew verb is often transitive and also neuter, so the place admits two interpretations; on the first, God is pressed beneath them as a wagon groans under too much weight, which he supports by another prophet's complaint that he was weighed down and constrained to labour under their sins. He calls that sense not unsuitable, but reports that the more received interpretation is behold, I will bind you fast as a wagon is bound, and in the end he prefers the active reading on two grounds: no necessity constrains us to take the same verb in two senses within one verse, active in the first clause and neuter in the second, and on the passive reading the comparison seems not quite suitable.

Ellicott reaches the same conclusion by a different route and names the parties. Three authorities support the passive rendering, the corresponding form in the next clause being taken the same way; but it is unlikely that God should declare himself crushed under the weight of Israel's sin, since in the context it is Israel and not God who is described as the victim. He adds that grammatical usage is against taking the word as passive, and that it does not favour the rendering press you down proposed by two other scholars either. Clarke prefers the marginal reading and works the picture out: God will bring over them the wheel of destruction, and it shall grind their place, their city and their temple, as a cart laden with sheaves presses down the ground and gravel and stones over which it rolls.

The catalogue of those who cannot escape is glossed briskly and read as a single argument. Gill supplies the reason in each case: they should be so straitened and cooped up and loaded with pressures that even one as swift as the runner famed for speed could not escape by fleeing, and the archer, who can use his weapon at a distance, will not think it safe to stand his ground but will take to his heels. Wesley gives the same in three strokes, that the enemies shall be swifter than they, that natural strength of body shall not deliver, and that the mighty means the valiant man of greatest courage. Clarke states the conclusion the list is driving at: none by might or counsel or fleetness shall escape, God having so fully determined to avenge the quarrel of his broken covenant that all attempts to escape his judgments shall be useless. He then makes a formal suggestion about the whole passage, that these sayings are proverbs, chosen to show the inutility of every attempt to escape the doom now decreed, even in the best circumstances, because the cup of their iniquity was full.

Ellicott is briefer than anyone here and says only what the doom is: an invasion and military overthrow, with all its attendant calamities, darkly foreshadowed. Keil and Delitzsch give the sequence without comment, the flight perishing from the swift, the strong unable to strengthen his force, the mighty and the archer and the horseman each unable to deliver himself, and the courageous fleeing away naked in that day. Gill closes on the last figure, the man strong in his heart, famous for courage and bravery, who excels among the mighty, the most valiant of soldiers and officers.
